title: Choosing the best value
objectives: Solve an optimisation problem stated in words.
Build the function from a constraint, then check the type and the ends.

screens.prose: You have 40 m of fencing for a rectangular pen against a long wall. The wall is the fourth side, so the fence makes two widths and one length.

derive.caption: Width {{fixed(w, 1)}} m, length {{fixed(40 - 2 * w, 1)}} m, area {{fixed(w * (40 - 2 * w), 1)}} m²

screens.question: Slide the width $w$ to make the area of the pen as large as possible.

hints.text: Watch the area in the caption as you slide.
The length along the wall is $40 - 2w$. Very narrow and very wide pens both have small areas.
Try $w = 8$, 10 and 12. The middle one gives the most.

feedback.correct: Width 10 m and length 20 m give 200 m².
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep sliding and watch the area: it rises, peaks, then falls.

byKey.square: You made the pen nearly square. With a wall as one side, a square gives about 178 m². A longer pen does better.

explain.text: The length is $40 - 2w$, so the area is $A(w) = w(40 - 2w)$. Width 10 gives $10 \times 20 = 200$ m², more than any other width. The pen is not square, because the wall saves one side.

screens.prose: The curve shows the area $A(w) = w(40 - 2w)$ for every width. Drag P along it and watch the tangent.
screens.question: Drag P to the top of the curve. What is the slope of the tangent there?

options.why: You read the height of the curve. The slope measures how steeply it climbs, and at the top it is flat.
40 is the slope at $w = 0$, where the pen has no area. The slope falls as $w$ grows.

hints.text: Read the slope in the caption as P reaches the highest point.
The top of the curve is at $w = 10$.

feedback.correct: The best width is a stationary point of $A$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put P at the top and read the slope in the caption.

explain.text: At $w = 10$ the slope is 0. The best width is a stationary point of $A$: $A'(w) = 40 - 4w = 0$ gives $w = 10$.

screens.prose: Building the function and finding where its slope is 0 is called **optimisation**. Try it on a box. Cut a square of side $x$ cm from each corner of a 30 cm card. Then fold up the sides.
screens.question: The volume is $V(x) = x(30 - 2x)^2$. Which cut $x$ gives the largest volume?

hints.text: Use the product rule on $x(30 - 2x)^2$, with the chain rule for the square.
$V'(x) = (30 - 2x)(30 - 6x)$, which is 0 at $x = 15$ or $x = 5$. At $x = 15$ the box is flat.

feedback.correct: A 5 cm cut gives a 20 by 20 by 5 box.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $V'(x) = 0$ and keep the solution that gives a real box.

byKey.other-root: You took $x = 15$, the other solution of $V'(x) = 0$. There the base has no width, so the volume is 0.
byKey.quarter: A 7.5 cm cut gives $7.5 \times 15^2 = 1687.5$ cm³, less than at 5 cm. Solve $V'(x) = 0$ rather than guess.

explain.text: $V'(x) = (30 - 2x)(30 - 6x)$ is 0 at $x = 5$ and $x = 15$. At 15 the box is flat, so the best cut is 5 cm. The box is 20 by 20 by 5: 2000 cm³.

screens.prose: An open box has a square base of side $x$ cm and height $h$ cm. It must hold 32,000 cm³, so $x^2 h = 32{,}000$. We want the least card: the area is $S = x^2 + 4xh$.

state.caption: Open box: square base $x$ by $x$, height $h$, no lid

screens.question: Write $S$ in terms of $x$ alone.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $h$ in terms of $x$ from $x^2 h = 32{,}000$, then substitute.

byKey.one-side: You turned $4xh$ into $\tfrac{32{,}000}{x}$, one side only. There are four sides: $4x \cdot \tfrac{32{,}000}{x^2}$.
byKey.lid: You gave the box a lid. It is open, so the base is the only $x^2$.

explain.text: From $x^2 h = 32{,}000$, $h = \tfrac{32{,}000}{x^2}$. Then $4xh = \tfrac{128{,}000}{x}$, so $S(x) = x^2 + \tfrac{128{,}000}{x}$. The constraint turned two unknowns into one.

screens.prose: Now differentiate $S(x) = x^2 + 128{,}000x^{-1}$ and set the slope to 0. The curve shows $S$ for each base side.
screens.question: Which base side $x$ uses the least card?

byKey.forgot-2: You solved $x^3 = 128{,}000$. The derivative of $x^2$ is $2x$, so $2x^3 = 128{,}000$ and $x^3 = 64{,}000$.
byKey.height: 20 cm is the height at the best size. The base side is 40 cm.

screens.prose: $x = 40$ makes $S'(x) = 0$. Before we trust it, we check its type and the ends of the range. Here $x$ can be any positive length.
screens.question: How do we know $x = 40$ gives the least card, not the most?

options.text: $S''(40) = 6 > 0$, and $S$ grows without bound near 0 and far out

options.why: A flat tangent alone could be a peak, a trough or neither. You need $S''$ or the signs of $S'$.

options.text: We still need to compare it with the end $x = 0$
options.why: There is no end to check. As $x \to 0$ the walls grow very tall and $S \to \infty$.

options.text: $S''(40) = 6 > 0$ means it is the most card
options.why: You read positive as a peak. $S'' > 0$ means the curve bends up: a trough.

hints.text: $S''(40) = 2 + 4 = 6 > 0$: a minimum. And $x > 0$ has no ends to compare.

feedback.correct: A local minimum, with nothing lower anywhere else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the type with $S''$, then think about what happens near 0 and far out.

explain.text: $S''(40) = 6 > 0$ makes $x = 40$ a local minimum. The range $x > 0$ has no ends, and $S$ shoots up near 0 and far out. So this local minimum is the least value overall.

screens.prose: Same 40 m of fence, but the wall is only 16 m long. The side along the wall, $40 - 2w$, can be at most 16 m.
screens.question: Which width $w$ now gives the largest area?

widget.label: Width in metres
widget.accept: 12 m, at the end of the allowed range.

hints.text: On $12 \le w \le 20$ the area only falls, so the best width is the end $w = 12$.

feedback.correct: $w = 12$: a pen 12 m by 16 m, 192 m².
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the allowed widths first, then look for the best one among them.

byKey.stationary: You used the stationary point. At $w = 10$ the side along the wall is 20 m, longer than the wall.
byKey.wall: 16 m is the side along the wall. The width solves $40 - 2w = 16$.

explain.text: $w = 10$ is outside the allowed range $12 \le w \le 20$, where $A$ only falls. So the best width is the end, $w = 12$: a pen 12 m by 16 m, area 192 m². When the stationary point is ruled out, the answer sits at an end.

screens.prose: Every problem followed the same steps: $$\text{choose } x \to \text{use the constraint} \to f(x) \to f'(x) = 0 \to \text{check type and ends}$$ The constraint removes the second unknown. The last step catches a stationary point of the wrong type or outside the range.
screens.question: You found $f'(a) = 0$ with $a$ inside a closed interval. What must you still do?

options.text: Check that $a$ is the type you want, and compare $f(a)$ with the ends

options.why: The box had $V'(15) = 0$ with zero volume. A flat point can be the wrong type.
The ends matter, but so does the type: $V'(15) = 0$ was the smallest volume, not the largest.

hints.text: Think of the box's $x = 15$ and of the 16 m wall.
$x = 15$ was the wrong type, and $w = 10$ lost to an end. Both checks are needed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the box's second root and the short wall.

explain.text: The box's $x = 15$ was a stationary point giving zero volume, the wrong type. The short wall's best width sat at an end. So check the type and compare with the ends.

screens.prose: With $L$ metres of fence against a wall, the area is $A(w) = w(L - 2w)$. $$A(w) = Lw - 2w^2 \quad \text{(expand)}$$ $$A'(w) = L - 4w \quad \text{(power rule)}$$ $$A'(w) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; w = \;?$$
screens.question: Complete the last line: the best width in terms of $L$.

widget.label: Best width in terms of L

hints.text: $4w = L$, so divide both sides by 4.

feedback.correct: $w = \tfrac{L}{4}$: a quarter of the fence on each width.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $L - 4w = 0$ and solve for $w$.

byKey.square: $\tfrac{L}{3}$ makes the three fenced sides equal. That is not where $A'(w) = 0$: solve $L - 4w = 0$.
byKey.half: At $w = \tfrac{L}{2}$ the side along the wall is $L - 2w = 0$: no pen at all.

explain.text: $L - 4w = 0$ gives $w = \tfrac{L}{4}$, and $A''(w) = -4 < 0$ makes it a maximum. The best area is $\tfrac{L}{4} \cdot \tfrac{L}{2} = \tfrac{L^2}{8}$. With $L = 40$ that is 10 m and 200 m², as you found.

screens.prose: A bet pays even money and wins with probability 0.6. You stake a fraction $f$ of your bankroll on each bet. The long-run growth rate per bet is $$G(f) = 0.6\ln(1 + f) + 0.4\ln(1 - f).$$
screens.question: Which fraction $f$ makes the growth rate $G$ largest?

hints.text: Differentiate each log with the chain rule.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\dfrac{0.6}{1 + f} = \dfrac{0.4}{1 - f}$.

byKey.p: You staked the chance of winning. At $f = 0.6$ the growth rate is negative: drag P there and see.
byKey.all: Staking everything risks ruin: $\ln(1 - f) \to -\infty$ as $f \to 1$.
byKey.half-p: At $f = 0.3$ the slope is already negative, so the growth rate is falling. Solve $G'(f) = 0$.

explain.text: $G'(f) = 0$ gives $0.6(1 - f) = 0.4(1 + f)$, so $f = 0.2$, and $G'' < 0$ makes it a maximum. For a bet paying $b$ to 1 the same steps give the **Kelly fraction** $f^* = p - \tfrac{q}{b}$. Staking more grows the bankroll more slowly: at $f = 0.4$ it shrinks.

ideas: Write the quantity as a function of one variable, using the constraint to remove the other.
Solve $f'(x) = 0$, then check the type with $f''$ or the signs of $f'$.
If the stationary point is outside the allowed range, the best value sits at an end.

formula.name: Kelly fraction
formula.note: It maximises $p\ln(1 + bf) + q\ln(1 - f)$ for a bet paying $b$ to 1.

summary.trap: A stationary point outside the allowed range is not the answer. With a 16 m wall, the best pen sat at the end $w = 12$.

quiz.prose: 60 m of fence makes a rectangular pen against a long wall. The wall is the fourth side.
quiz.question: What is the largest area the pen can have, in m²?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $A(w) = w(60 - 2w)$ and solve $A'(w) = 0$.

byKey.square: You made three equal sides of 20 m. The best pen is twice as long as it is wide: 15 by 30.
byKey.width-sq: You squared the best width. The length along the wall is $60 - 2 \times 15 = 30$ m.

explain.text: $A(w) = w(60 - 2w)$, so $A'(w) = 60 - 4w = 0$ at $w = 15$. The pen is 15 m by 30 m, an area of 450 m².

quiz.prose: An order of $q$ shares earns an expected £0.05 a share before costs. Market impact costs $0.000002q^2$ pounds, so expected profit is $\pi(q) = 0.05q - 0.000002q^2$.
quiz.question: Which order size $q$ maximises expected profit?

feedback.correct: 12,500 shares, for an expected profit of £312.50.

byKey.forgot-2: You solved $0.05 - 0.000002q = 0$. The derivative of $q^2$ is $2q$. At 25,000 shares the profit is back to 0.
byKey.quarter: At 6,250 shares the slope is still positive: $0.05 - 0.025 = 0.025$. A bigger order earns more.

explain.text: $\pi'(q) = 0.05 - 0.000004q = 0$ at $q = 12{,}500$, and $\pi''(q) < 0$ makes it a maximum. Expected profit there is $\text{£}625 - \text{£}312.50 = \text{£}312.50$.

quiz.prose: A bet pays 2 to 1, so $b = 2$, and wins with probability $p = 0.55$. The Kelly fraction is $f^* = p - \dfrac{q}{b}$.
quiz.question: What fraction of your bankroll should you stake?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $q = 1 - p = 0.45$ and divide it by $b = 2$.

byKey.p-minus-q: You left out $b$. The bet pays 2 to 1, so subtract $\tfrac{0.45}{2}$, not 0.45.
byKey.edge: 0.65 is the expected profit per £1 staked, $pb - q$. Kelly divides it by $b$.
byKey.p: You staked the chance of winning. The losing chance pulls the stake down: subtract $\tfrac{q}{b}$.

explain.text: $q = 0.45$, so $f^* = 0.55 - \tfrac{0.45}{2} = 0.325$. Equivalently $f^* = \tfrac{pb - q}{b} = \tfrac{0.65}{2}$: the edge divided by the odds.

quiz.prose: A cost is $C(x) = x + \dfrac{100}{x}$, and $x$ must lie in $1 \le x \le 5$.
quiz.question: What is the smallest cost on this interval?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where $C'(x) = 0$, check it is in range, then compare the ends.

byKey.left-end: That is the largest cost, at $x = 1$. The cost falls all the way to $x = 5$.

explain.text: $C'(x) = 1 - \tfrac{100}{x^2} = 0$ at $x = 10$, outside the range. On $1 \le x \le 5$, $C'(x) < 0$, so $C$ falls throughout. The smallest cost is at the end: $C(5) = 25$.
